questions.question_text: Friction force opposes:
questions.explanation: Friction acts to resist sliding or attempted sliding.

questions.question_text: The friction formula is:
questions.explanation: Friction equals coefficient times normal force.

questions.question_text: Static friction is the friction when an object is:
questions.explanation: Static friction prevents motion until a threshold is exceeded.

questions.question_text: Increasing the mass of an object on a horizontal surface increases:
questions.explanation: On a level surface, N ≈ mg increases with mass.

questions.question_text: Friction enables walking by providing a forward push from the ground.
questions.explanation: Without friction, feet would slip backward.

questions.question_text: A rougher surface generally has:
questions.explanation: Roughness increases μ for many material pairs.

questions.question_text: Kinetic friction acts when:
options: Surfaces slide relative to each other
Object is at rest on a slope below threshold
questions.correct_answer: Surfaces slide relative to each other
questions.explanation: Kinetic friction applies during sliding motion.

questions.question_text: Friction always converts some mechanical energy to thermal energy.
questions.explanation: Sliding friction dissipates energy as heat.

questions.question_text: Name the two types of friction discussed in the simulation.
questions.explanation: Static friction before sliding; kinetic during sliding.

questions.question_text: What symbol represents the coefficient of friction?
questions.explanation: Mu (μ) is the coefficient of friction.

questions.question_text: The period of a simple pendulum depends mainly on:
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(L/g) for small angles.

questions.question_text: Increasing pendulum length while g is constant:
questions.explanation: Longer L gives longer period.

questions.question_text: On the Moon (weaker g), the same pendulum has:
questions.explanation: Smaller g increases T = 2π√(L/g).

questions.question_text: For small angles, changing bob mass:
questions.explanation: Ideal pendulum period is independent of mass.

questions.question_text: A pendulum converts energy between gravitational PE and KE.
questions.explanation: Energy oscillates between potential and kinetic forms.

questions.question_text: Measuring 10 complete oscillations and dividing by 10 gives:
questions.explanation: Timing multiple oscillations improves period accuracy.

questions.question_text: Frequency is related to period by:
questions.explanation: Frequency is the reciprocal of period.

questions.question_text: Very large release angles violate the small-angle approximation for period.
questions.explanation: Large angles make actual period longer than 2π√(L/g) predicts.

questions.question_text: Write the formula for period of a simple pendulum.
questions.explanation: Period depends on length and gravitational field strength.

questions.question_text: Name one variable you can change in the Pendulum Lab simulation.
questions.explanation: Length, mass, gravity, and initial angle can be adjusted.

questions.question_text: Momentum is defined as:
questions.explanation: p = mv defines linear momentum.

questions.question_text: The Law of Conservation of Momentum states that total momentum in a closed system:
questions.explanation: Total momentum before equals total after if no external impulse.

questions.question_text: In an elastic collision:
questions.explanation: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and KE.

questions.question_text: In a perfectly inelastic collision, objects:
options: Stick together and move as one
questions.correct_answer: Stick together and move as one
questions.explanation: Inelastic collisions often combine objects after impact.

questions.question_text: Momentum is a vector quantity.
questions.explanation: Momentum has both magnitude and direction.

questions.question_text: Doubling the velocity of a puck quadruples its:
options: Both momentum and KE as stated
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv² scales with v²; momentum p = mv scales linearly with v.

questions.question_text: If two identical pucks approach with equal speed and opposite direction, total momentum before collision is:
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite momenta cancel.

questions.question_text: Kinetic energy is always conserved in every collision.
questions.explanation: Only elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy.

questions.question_text: Write the formula for momentum.
questions.explanation: Momentum equals mass times velocity.

questions.question_text: Name one collision mode available in the simulation.
questions.explanation: Elastic and inelastic modes can be selected.

questions.question_text: Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet run from:
options: North to south outside the magnet
questions.correct_answer: North to south outside the magnet
questions.explanation: Field lines emerge from north and enter south externally.

questions.question_text: A current-carrying coil produces:
questions.explanation: Moving charges in a coil create a magnetic field.

questions.question_text: Reversing the current in an electromagnet:
questions.explanation: Current direction determines field direction.

questions.question_text: Increasing the number of coil turns:
questions.explanation: More turns increase the magnetic field for the same current.

questions.question_text: A compass needle aligns with the local magnetic field direction.
questions.explanation: The needle is a small magnet aligning with external fields.

questions.question_text: Electromagnets are used in devices such as:
questions.explanation: Electromagnets allow switchable magnetic fields.

questions.question_text: The right-hand rule helps determine:
options: Direction of magnetic field around a current
questions.correct_answer: Direction of magnetic field around a current
questions.explanation: Thumb along current, fingers curl in field direction.

questions.question_text: Increasing current through the coil strengthens the electromagnet.
questions.explanation: Stronger current produces a stronger magnetic field.

questions.question_text: Name the two poles of a bar magnet.
questions.explanation: Magnets have north and south poles.

questions.question_text: What tool in the simulation shows field direction near a magnet?
questions.explanation: A compass needle deflects in magnetic fields.

questions.question_text: Density is defined as:
questions.explanation: ρ = m/V.

questions.question_text: An object floats in water if its density is:
questions.explanation: Less dense objects displace enough fluid to support their weight.

questions.question_text: If mass doubles while volume stays the same, density:
questions.explanation: ρ = m/V, so density is proportional to mass at fixed volume.

questions.question_text: The SI unit of density is:
questions.explanation: Density is mass divided by volume.

questions.question_text: Objects with density greater than water sink.
questions.explanation: Average density greater than the fluid leads to sinking.

questions.question_text: In Mystery Blocks mode, density helps:
questions.explanation: Measured density can be compared to reference values.

questions.question_text: Two blocks of the same material have:
options: The same density regardless of size
questions.correct_answer: The same density regardless of size
questions.explanation: Density is a material property at constant temperature.

questions.question_text: Density describes how tightly matter is packed in a substance.
questions.explanation: Higher density means more mass in the same volume.

questions.question_text: Write the formula for density.
questions.explanation: Density equals mass divided by volume.

questions.question_text: Will a block less dense than water float or sink?
questions.explanation: Lower density than the fluid gives buoyant support for floating.
